How much to charge for a photo booth rental

Most photo booth pricing advice answers a question nobody can use: what the market charges. The number that decides whether a booking is worth taking is what this booking costs you — and that figure is larger than it looks, for two reasons a package price never mentions.

Open the free quote calculator

A 3-hour booking is 5 hours 25 minutes of your day

The hours on the package are the hours a guest sees the booth open. The hours you commit are longer:

Committed timeMinutes
Booth open (the hours on the package)180
Setup — unpack, backdrop, lighting, test prints60
Teardown — pack down and load out45
Round-trip drive40
Total committed325 (5 hours 25 minutes)

That is 4.75 hours on site and 5.42 hours committed against 3 hours sold. An operator pricing on the booked figure is pricing away 45% of the day the booking actually consumes — which is why a fully booked weekend can still fail to pay.

Worked example: pricing one booking

A three-hour Saturday event, one attendant at a $25/hour target rate, 24 round-trip miles at $0.67, an expected 150 prints at $0.35 each, $20 of props, $35 of amortized equipment, a 15% peak-day premium on labor and travel, 10% overhead, and a 35% target margin:

LineAmount
Labor (5.42 committed hours × $25)$135.42
Mileage (24 × $0.67)$16.08
Peak-day premium (15% of labor and travel)$22.72
Prints (150 × $0.35)$52.50
Props and backdrop$20.00
Equipment, amortized per event$35.00
Direct cost$281.72
Overhead (10%)$22.92
Total cost — your break-even$304.64
Price at a 35% margin$468.68
Profit$164.04
Profit per committed hour$30.28

Note the two hourly figures this produces. The price works out to $156.23 per booked hour, which is the number that appears on a competitor's website. The profit is $30.28 per committed hour, which is the number that tells you whether the Saturday was worth giving up.

The unlimited-print trap

The quote above assumes 150 prints. Nothing in it obliges the event to cooperate. Run the same booking at 450 prints — a well-attended wedding rather than a quiet corporate evening — and only one line moves:

Line150 prints450 prints
Print cost$52.50$157.50
Total cost$304.64$409.64
Price charged$468.68$468.68
Profit$164.04$59.04
Prints as a share of cost11.2%25.0%

The price never moved and the profit fell by 64%. This is the structural problem with unlimited prints: the busiest, most successful, most-referred events are the expensive ones to serve, and the package price rewards you the same either way. The calculator flags this as a print-volume risk once prints pass a quarter of direct cost, which is roughly where a normal event-to-event swing starts costing more than the margin can absorb.

There are two honest fixes and one bad habit. Cap the prints, or charge per print above an allotment, and the variable cost sits with whoever controls it. Or quote from a realistic busy-case estimate rather than an average, giving up some quiet-event margin to never be caught out. The bad habit is quoting the optimistic number and hoping, because the events most likely to run over are exactly the ones you most wanted to win.

The four costs most often left out

Setup and teardown, because it does not feel like the job. Drive time, which is committed labor and not merely fuel — mileage covers the vehicle, not the hour of your life. Equipment amortization, because the booth and printer were bought once and therefore feel free per event, when they are a replacement cost spread over the bookings they will serve. And overhead — insurance, storage, software, marketing — which is a real percentage of every job even though no line on the event names it.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a photo booth rental?

Price the hours you actually commit, not the hours on the package. Add setup, teardown, and round-trip drive time to the booked hours, cost that whole block at what you need to earn per hour, then add mileage, prints, props, amortized equipment, a peak-day premium if it applies, and overhead. Divide the resulting cost by one minus your target margin. In the worked example on this page a 3-hour booking works out to 5 hours 25 minutes of committed time, costs 304.64 dollars all in, and needs a price of 468.68 dollars to leave a 35 percent margin.

Why is a 3-hour photo booth booking really more than 3 hours?

Because the booked hours are only the hours a guest sees the booth open. An hour of setup for unpacking, backdrop, lighting and test prints, 45 minutes of teardown and loading, and 40 minutes of round-trip drive are all time you cannot sell to anyone else. That is 5 hours 25 minutes of committed time against 3 hours of booked time. Pricing on the booked figure prices away nearly half your day, and it is the single most common reason a fully booked weekend still does not pay.

How do unlimited prints affect photo booth pricing?

They turn a fixed price into a variable cost you do not control. Paper and ribbon scale with how many guests actually use the booth, so a busy event costs more to serve than a quiet one at exactly the same price. In the worked example, quoting 468.68 dollars on an expected 150 prints leaves 164.04 dollars of profit; if that event turns busy and produces 450 prints, print cost rises from 52.50 dollars to 157.50 dollars and the profit falls to 59.04 dollars. The price never moved and the profit dropped by nearly two thirds.

Should I cap prints or price for the busy case?

Either works as long as you choose deliberately. Capping prints, or charging per print above an allotment, keeps the variable cost with the person who controls it. Pricing for the busy case means quoting off a realistic high print estimate rather than an average one, which costs you some quiet-event margin in exchange for never being caught out. What does not work is quoting off an optimistic estimate and hoping, because the events most likely to run over are the large, well-attended ones you most wanted to win.

What costs do photo booth operators most often leave out of a quote?

Four, in roughly this order. Setup and teardown time, because it does not feel like the job. Round-trip drive time, which is committed labor and not only fuel. Equipment amortization, because the booth, camera and printer were bought once and so feel free per event, when they are really a replacement cost spread across the bookings they will serve. And overhead such as insurance, storage, software and marketing, which is a real percentage of every job even though no line item on the event names it.

How do I price a Saturday or holiday differently from a weeknight?

Add a peak premium to the labor and travel portion of the cost rather than to the whole quote. Those are the parts a peak date actually makes more expensive, because the same Saturday evening could have been sold to another client and your attendant is harder to staff. Print, props and equipment costs do not change with the day of the week. In the worked example a 15 percent peak premium on labor and travel adds 22.72 dollars, which is the honest size of that difference rather than a round number added to the total.

Run it on your own booking

The calculator takes every figure used above, reports your break-even and target price, shows profit per committed hour, and flags the print-volume risk before you send the quote. It runs entirely in your browser.

Common questions

Why count setup and teardown time when the guest only sees the booth running for the booked hours?

Because you and your equipment are committed to the job for that time too. A 3-hour package with an hour of setup and 45 minutes of teardown is 4.75 hours on site before travel — pricing only the 3 booked hours quietly cuts your real hourly rate every time.

Why does the calculator treat print cost as a risk, not just a cost line?

Unlimited-print packages are quoted from an estimated print count, but the actual count depends on how many guests show up and use the booth — a busy open bar can print far more strips than a seated dinner. The calculator reports what share of your price the print line already represents, so you can see how much room is left before extra prints erase the margin you built the quote on.

How is the recommended overtime rate different from just charging my hourly rate for the extra time?

It marks the extra hour up the same way the rest of the quote is marked up — attendant pay plus your overhead rate, divided by your target margin — so an event that runs long still earns the same margin instead of just covering the added labor at cost.

Does anything about my event details get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing you type is saved anywhere — it exists only in the page while it is open. The shareable link is the one thing that travels, and only when you press the button for it: it carries your numbers inside the URL itself rather than uploading them anywhere, so whoever you send it to opens the same quote — send it only to the person you are quoting. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

This calculator vs. a flat "3-hour, $500" photo booth package

"3-hour, $500" is not a price for a photo booth booking — it is a price for one nearby, modestly-printed, single-attendant event, quietly applied to every booking the calendar takes.

What a flat "3-hour, $500" package is

A flat package is the fastest way to sell a booking: one headline number on a website or an Instagram post, read off and repeated. Couples and event planners shop it because it is easy to compare between vendors, and it is the number a client holding a competitor's price sheet will ask you to match on their own event.

The number behind it was set for one booking — usually the cheapest configuration this calculator prices (a short drive, one attendant, a modest print estimate) — and then reused for every 3-hour booking afterward, whether or not the next event looks anything like that one.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the booked hours, setup and teardown minutes, round-trip drive time and mileage, attendant count and pay, expected prints and cost per print, props and equipment cost, and your target margin. It prices the labor, the travel, and the print-volume risk separately, and returns a walk-away price for the booking you describe — for this event, not a generic one.

Booking$500 packageWalk-away priceVerdict
Base case: 24-mi round trip, 1 attendant, 150 prints$500.00$468.68Covers it, $31.32 to spare
Busy open bar: 40-mi round trip, 1 attendant, 400 prints$500.00$640.38Loses $140.38
Saturday wedding: 60-mi round trip, 2 attendants, 500 prints$500.00$1,032.50Loses $532.50

All three are the same 3 booked hours (60 minutes setup, 45 minutes teardown, 15% weekend/holiday premium), worked using this calculator's own form defaults — $25/hr attendant pay, $0.35/print, $20 props, $35 equipment, 10% overhead, 35% target margin — not numbers invented for this page. Open the calculator and check any row yourself.

What a flat package doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $500 whether the venue is a 10-minute drive or an hour away, and whether one attendant staffs it or two — several times the labor and mileage for the same words "3-hour package". Prices round-trip drive time and mileage from the entered numbers, and multiplies labor by attendant count, so bookings of different scope come out at different numbers instead of one.
Prices "unlimited prints" as a fixed line item, with no separate field for how busy the event turns out to be — a seated dinner and an open bar quote the same. Times an entered print estimate by cost per print, and reports what share of the price that line already represents, so a print-heavy event shows up instead of being absorbed into the package.
Prices only the hours a guest sees the booth running, with no line for the setup before doors open or the teardown after they close. Adds setup and teardown minutes to the booked hours before pricing labor, so the attendant's full committed time is charged, not just the visible hours.
Applies a weekend or holiday premium inconsistently, if at all, since there is no separate line to apply it to. Applies the entered weekend/holiday premium to labor and mileage cost specifically, so a peak date is priced differently from a weeknight.
Gives the operator a price to sell, not a number to check a quote against when a client asks to match a cheaper flat rate on a farther, busier event. Reports a walk-away price built from the entered scope, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the booking is confirmed.

A flat package is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one booking it was built for, and nothing about a posted price tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat package skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat "3-hour, $500" photo booth package get the price wrong?

Because the real cost of a booking scales with setup and teardown time, travel distance, attendant count, and how many prints the event actually produces, not with the phrase "3-hour package" alone. A quiet Tuesday corporate dinner close to base is a different booking from a Saturday open-bar wedding an hour's drive away with a second attendant, even though both are sold as the same 3-hour package. A flat price quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat package price usually leave out entirely?

Setup and teardown time, the drive to the venue, and print-volume risk. A published package price is set on the cheapest configuration -- an hour of setup, 45 minutes of teardown, a short drive, one attendant, and a modest print estimate -- and has nowhere to put the extra hours and paper and ink cost of a farther venue, a second attendant, or an open bar that prints far more strips than a seated dinner. An operator pricing off the package alone finds out about the gap only after the event.

How much do travel, a second attendant, and print volume actually add over the flat package?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at the form's own default rates ($25/hr attendant pay, $0.35/print, 10% overhead, 35% target margin): the booking a $500 package is actually sized for -- a 24-mile round trip, one attendant, 150 prints -- walks away at $468.68, comfortably inside the package price. A busier open-bar event at the same 3 booked hours but a 40-mile round trip and 400 prints walks away at $640.38, $140.38 over the package. A Saturday wedding with a second attendant, a 60-mile round trip, and 500 prints walks away at $1,032.50, $532.50 over the package. Travel, attendant count, and print volume -- not the phrase "3-hour package" -- are what move the number.

Is a flat package price ever the right way to quote a booking?

For the one booking it was actually priced on, yes -- this calculator's own default job, a nearby venue with one attendant and a modest print count, walks away under the $500 package price. The package breaks down once a booking moves away from that base case: farther travel, a second attendant, or a busier open bar all add real committed time and print cost that a flat package was never sized to cover.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the booked hours, setup/teardown time, travel, attendant count and pay, expected prints, and your target margin, and turns them into a walk-away price for the booking you describe -- the arithmetic a flat package skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat "3-hour, $500" package is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works for the booking it was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. Photobooth Supply Co's Profit Calculator

One tool asks whether a photo booth business could work in your market. This one prices the booking you already have. They are useful at different points in the business, not competing answers to the same question.

What each one is for

Photobooth Supply Co's Profit Calculator is a free lead tool published by Photobooth Supply Co, a photo booth equipment and business-management-software vendor. It estimates how profitable a photo booth business could be for you from local search volume and an assumed booking rate for your area, with sensible defaults if you are not sure of your own numbers, and emails the projection to the address you provide. It is aimed at someone deciding whether to start a photo booth business, or how much a new market could be worth, not at pricing a specific event that is already on the calendar.

This calculator does the other job: it prices one booking you already have. It takes the booked hours, the setup and teardown time on either side of them, travel, attendant labor, the props and equipment cost, and the print-volume risk an unlimited-print package carries, and turns that into a real price at your own target margin — then checks a number you are already considering against the breakeven. A market-sizing average has no field for any of that, because it is not trying to answer that question.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Could a photo booth business be profitable in my area?Photobooth Supply Co's Profit Calculator — a market-sizing estimate from local search volume and an assumed booking rate.
I have a date and a venue. What should I actually charge for it?This calculator — free, private, no account, no email.
How much does setup, teardown, and the drive to this venue actually cost me?This calculator. A market average has no field for one event's specific time and distance.
How much room is left in an unlimited-print package before a busy open bar erases the margin?This calculator's print-volume check — not something a business-level average estimates.
Do I need to give up my email address to see the number?This calculator: no. Photobooth Supply Co's tool sends its projection by email.
Price your own booking

This calculator needs no account, no email, and no upload: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is sent anywhere or saved when you close the tab.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Photobooth Supply Co's Profit Calculator?

They answer different questions. Photobooth Supply Co, a photo booth equipment and business-software vendor, publishes a free Profit Calculator that estimates how profitable a photo booth business could be in your area from local search volume and assumed booking rates, and emails you the projection — a market-sizing tool aimed at someone deciding whether to start or grow a booth business. This calculator instead prices one booking you already have: the hours, setup and teardown time, travel, attendant labor, print cost, and equipment cost behind that specific event, checked against your target margin. If you are deciding whether the business is worth starting, their market estimate is the right tool. If you already have a date and a venue and need a real number to quote, this one is.

Does this calculator need my email or an account?

No. Photobooth Supply Co's Profit Calculator asks for an email address to send you the projection. This tool needs neither an email nor an account — it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is sent anywhere or saved when you close the tab.

Does a business-level profit estimate already cover one booking's real cost?

No, and it is not built to. A market-sizing estimate works from an assumed average booking rate and volume for an area — it has no field for one event's specific setup and teardown time, drive distance, attendant labor, or how much of an unlimited-print package's paper and ink a busy open bar will actually burn through versus a quiet dinner. Those are exactly the numbers this calculator asks for, because they are what determine whether one booking, priced at a given number, actually clears its costs.

Is this page affiliated with Photobooth Supply Co?

No. This page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Photobooth Supply Co. Photobooth Supply Co and Profit Calculator are named here only to describe what this tool is and is not.
